title: The Machine Age Fund | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z raised $1.1B for a new Machine Age Fund dedicated to the physical AI stack (chips, memory, networking, power, data centers, robotics), arguing that compute density, power demand, and supply-chain growth rates must jump by orders of magnitude to keep pace with AI demand.

insights.claim: a16z raised $1.1B for a new vehicle, the Machine Age Fund, dedicated to investing across the full physical AI stack: chips, memory, networking, storage, data centers, robotics, and home AI appliances.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
insights.so_what: Signals a major new pool of capital targeting AI physical infrastructure (semis, power, data centers, robotics) rather than software applications — relevant for tracking capital flows into the AI hardware supply chain.
insights.quote: We’ve raised $1.1B for a16z’s newest fund: the Machine Age Fund.

insights.claim: The authors argue that as AI shifts from chat to reasoning to coding and other knowledge work, both the demand for AI work and the token intensity of that work rise by orders of magnitude, a trend they describe as machine intelligence 'going vertical.'
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
insights.so_what: Frames token/compute demand growth as accelerating rather than linear, underpinning the bull case for compute and power infrastructure investment.

insights.claim: The authors use a framework of compute epochs (mainframe to client-server, to internet, cloud, and mobile) to argue infrastructure reinvention is a recurring pattern, but claim the current AI epoch requires far greater magnitude, breadth, and speed of change than prior transitions.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
insights.so_what: Provides a lens for evaluating whether current AI infra capex is a bubble or a genuine platform shift comparable to past compute-era transitions.
insights.quote: Reinventions like this happen at each epoch of compute, from the shift from mainframe to client server, to the Internet, cloud and mobile.
insights.locator: Reinventions like this happen at each epoch

insights.claim: The fund frames AI physical infrastructure buildout as a 'social and national imperative,' not merely a commercial opportunity, echoing the political/national-security framing a16z has used for its American Dynamism practice.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
insights.so_what: Suggests a16z is positioning AI hardware investment alongside defense/reindustrialization themes, which may attract policy tailwinds, government-adjacent deals, and co-investment from strategic/defense capital.
insights.quote: It is our social and national imperative.

insights.claim: Compute density per server rack increased 28x moving from an Nvidia H100-generation rack to a Rubin-generation rack, illustrating how fast physical infrastructure must scale to keep up with AI chip generations.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
insights.so_what: A 28x rack-density jump implies proportionate stress on power, cooling, and networking supply chains — a leading indicator for demand in those sub-sectors.
insights.quote: Compute density per rack increased by 28X from an H100 rack to a Rubin rack.

insights.claim: Intra-rack networking is hitting the physical limits of copper cabling as rack compute density scales, implying growing need for alternative interconnect technologies (e.g., optical) to sustain further density increases.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
insights.so_what: Watch for investment and demand acceleration in optical interconnect and next-gen networking startups as copper becomes a bottleneck inside AI racks.
insights.quote: Networking within a rack has grown similarly, hitting the limits of copper cabling

insights.claim: Rack power draw moved from roughly 5-10 kW to 100-250 kW to support current AI systems, and the authors predict it will rise to 1 MW per rack within three years.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
insights.so_what: A roughly 100x-plus rise in per-rack power density within three years implies massive incremental demand for power delivery, cooling, and grid/behind-the-meter generation equipment — a direct read-through for power and cooling infrastructure investors.
insights.quote: Rack power moved from roughly 5-10 kW to 100-250 kW to support today’s systems and will increase to 1MW over the next 3 years.

insights.claim: Data center scale is shifting from tens/hundreds of megawatts to gigawatt-scale campuses in some cases, while power sourcing is shifting from grid-only supply to a mix including behind-the-meter or captive generation.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
insights.so_what: Signals growing investable opportunity in on-site/captive power generation (gas turbines, nuclear, fuel cells) for AI campuses, since grid capacity alone can't keep pace.
insights.quote: Power is increasingly supplied not only from grid-only to grid plus behind-the-meter or captive sources.

insights.claim: The hardware supply chain has historically grown at 20-30% per year at most, but the authors argue AI demand now requires triple-digit annual growth rates, and they expect this mismatch to resolve quickly.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
insights.so_what: Highlights a structural supply-demand gap in hardware manufacturing capacity that could sustain elevated pricing/margins for suppliers able to scale output, and creates opportunity for new entrants disrupting incumbent supply chains.
insights.quote: The hardware industry supply side is used to growing 20% to 30% per year at most; not the triple-digit growth that’s needed to catch up with demand. This will change, quickly.
insights.locator: We need faster, more efficient systems

themes.theme: a16z's hardware track record and strategic pivot

insights.claim: a16z's hardware-related startup deal flow grew from a small share to over 20% of total deal flow over the past couple of years, evidencing a sharp rise in founder activity targeting AI hardware.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
insights.so_what: A jump to over 20% hardware deal flow at a top-tier VC is a leading indicator that founder and capital interest is rotating meaningfully from software toward AI physical infrastructure.
insights.quote: Over the last couple of years we’ve seen hardware startups grow from a small amount of deal flow to now over 20%.

insights.claim: Ahead of formally launching the Machine Age Fund, a16z had already backed hardware startups including Unconventional AI, Nexthop, Volta, Atoms, Heron Power, and Mind Robotics.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
insights.so_what: Names specific portfolio companies (power, networking, robotics) worth tracking as bellwethers of a16z's Machine Age Fund thesis in practice.
insights.quote: Recently we’ve backed a number of hardware companies including Unconventional AI, Nexthop, Volta, Atoms, Heron Power and Mind Robotics.

insights.claim: a16z points to a track record in hardware predating this fund: leading the 2016 Series A in Skydio, investing in SpaceX, writing an early check into Anduril in 2019, and being among the first VC investors in Waymo's 2020 raise.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
insights.so_what: Establishes credibility/pattern-matching for the firm's new hardware fund by citing prior successful hard-tech bets (drones, space, defense, autonomy).
insights.quote: In 2016, we led the series A in Skydio; we invested in SpaceX; we wrote our first check into Anduril in 2019, and were among the first venture investors in Waymo’s 2020 raise.

insights.claim: Despite being widely known as software investors, a16z is now making hardware an official investing motion via the Machine Age Fund, marking a formal strategic expansion of the firm's identity and capital allocation beyond its software-centric brand.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
insights.so_what: A leading software-focused VC formally institutionalizing hardware investing suggests the AI capex cycle is durable enough to reshape even generalist VC firm strategy, not just specialist hardware funds.
insights.quote: While we at a16z are generally known as software investors, we have always paid attention to hardware.

insights.claim: The Machine Age Fund is staffed with senior hardware operating experience: Guido Appenzeller, formerly CTO of Intel's Data Center Group, alongside Raghu Raghuram and Martin Casado, who each spent multiple decades in data-center systems software requiring deep hardware partnership.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
insights.so_what: Deep bench of ex-operators (Intel's data center CTO among them) suggests the fund can underwrite technically complex hardware bets, not just financial ones — relevant for assessing execution risk on this thesis.
insights.quote: Guido Appenzeller was the CTO for Intel’s Data Center Group (DPG).
insights.locator: Hardware is in our team DNA

insights.claim: David Ulevitch and Erin Price-Wright's American Dynamism practice will lead much of the firm's hardware and U.S. manufacturing investing, tying the Machine Age Fund's activity to a16z's broader U.S. reindustrialization and defense-tech investment theme.
insights.speaker: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
insights.so_what: Links AI hardware capital flows to the American Dynamism/defense-tech ecosystem, implying overlap with government contracts, national-security-adjacent capital, and U.S. manufacturing policy tailwinds.
insights.quote: David Ulevitch and Erin Price-Wright lead many of the firm’s hardware and U.S. manufacturing investments through our American Dynamism practice.
insights.locator: Hardware is in our team DNA

source_meta.author: Ben Horowitz, Martin Casado, Raghu Raghuram, David Ulevitch, David George
